A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 rows toward higher y, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The baseline collapsed to DONE at the first step (episode length 1.0 by 50% of training). The traces suggest why. The target heights the agent observes are the true design shifted down by Y/2 = 4 rows, wrapping round (observed row r = design row (r+4) mod 8). Rewards follow the true design: in the untrained trace, a 1x2 at row 7, columns 6-7 scored -0.010, i.e. one cell in and one out of the real design. So the observation and the action grid are misaligned. A network of local convolutions with zero padding cannot link an observed cell to the action 4 rows away. Every placement then looks like noise with negative expected reward, and stopping at once (reward 0) wins. The fix should be perceptual: give the network either a copy of the observation shifted by Y/2 rows, or a learned layer that mixes all positions. Recipe changes such as more updates and more entropy may also help avoid the DONE collapse.

### Round 2
The observed target channels are rolled by Y/2 rows compared with the true design (the traces show this). The starting network could not line up targets with actions, so it collapsed to DONE at once. Feeding in an extra half-rolled copy of the observation fixed this. r1c1 scored 0.662 with both seeds steady. The r1c2 recipe (128 envs, 3 epochs, entropy 0.02) gave one seed 0.848, the best so far, and the other 0.078. So more updates can raise the ceiling, but results become unstable across seeds. The learned token-mixing layer (r1c3) could not learn the remap at this budget. Next steps: keep the rolled copy, and test which recipe changes give more updates without seed failures. One run changes only the update count. One adds the standard small-gain init on the policy outputs, which should give a near-uniform starting policy and resist DONE collapse. One trades PPO epochs for more samples.

### Round 3
The observed target is shifted by Y/2 rows. Adding a half-rolled copy of the input (r1c1) took the network from collapsing to DONE (0.0) to 0.66. A learned token-mixing layer could not learn this remap within the budget (r1c3, 0.0). Most of the remaining gain came from the recipe. Doubling the update count with 128 envs gave 0.86, with both seeds stable. Cutting PPO epochs to 2 buys 1.8 times more fresh samples and gave 0.93 (0.947 and 0.914), the best so far. Because every episode has a fresh design, sample count and update count seem to matter more than reusing samples. A small output init did not help (0.84). The best run has mean IoU 0.993, so its remaining failures are small errors, not missing skill. This round: 1 epoch, which gives about 1.75 times more samples again; 64 envs, which doubles the update count; and one architecture test, adding global context plus a wider receptive field.

### Round 4
Every working trial depends on the half-roll input. The target is observed shifted by Y/2 rows, and the learned token mixer (r1c3) could not learn that shift in time. Of the recipes, 128 envs with 2 epochs (r2c3) is best: 0.931, with both seeds fine. The main risk is the policy collapsing to choosing DONE straight away. Six of the 18 seed runs collapsed fully or partly: both seeds of r3c1 and r3c2, one of r1c2 and one of r3c3. These configurations have similar sample counts, so collapse looks largely random. The final pick is retrained on 4 new seeds, so lowering the collapse rate matters about as much as raising the mean. Early in training, random placements earn negative reward and DONE earns 0, so the DONE logit rises fast. A larger entropy bonus keeps probability spread over placements while they learn to aim at missing cells. A longer horizon makes the +1 exact-build bonus count for more, which may cut order mistakes. All three candidates keep the r2c3 network, so the results isolate the recipe.
